name: Data Structures
description: Arrays, hash tables, trees, heaps, graphs and tries — how they are built, what they cost, and when to pick which.

modules.name: Linear Structures
modules.description: Arrays, lists, stacks, queues and the cache behaviour that decides real performance.

cards.answer: Arrays give O(1) indexing and cache locality; linked lists give O(1) splice at a known node and stable references.

right.title: Linked list
points: Pointer chasing — a cache miss per node

cards.explanation: In practice arrays win far more often than the asymptotics suggest, because a cache miss costs ~100x an L1 hit. Linked lists earn their place when you hold stable node references, splice frequently, or need intrusive lists in kernels and allocators.

cards.prompt: Why is appending to a dynamic array amortised O(1) even though resizing is O(n)?
cards.answer: Because capacity grows geometrically. Doubling means the total copy work across n appends is n + n/2 + n/4 + … < 2n, so the average per append is constant.
cards.explanation: Growing by a constant amount instead would make n appends O(n²). The growth factor trades memory for copies: 2x wastes up to half the buffer, 1.5x reuses freed blocks better — which is why several implementations chose it.

cards.prompt: You are parsing nested brackets and separately scheduling jobs fairly. Which structure for each, and why?
cards.answer: A stack (LIFO) for the brackets — the most recent opener must close first. A queue (FIFO) for the jobs — fairness means first submitted, first served.
cards.explanation: Recursion is a stack; breadth-first traversal is a queue; depth-first is a stack. Recognising which discipline a problem needs usually solves half of it. A deque supports both ends and is the base for sliding-window algorithms.

cards.prompt: How do hash tables resolve collisions, and what is the load factor?
cards.answer: Separate chaining stores colliding entries in a per-bucket list or tree; open addressing probes for another slot (linear, quadratic or double hashing). Load factor = entries / buckets, and it drives the resize.
cards.explanation: Open addressing is cache-friendlier but degrades sharply past ~0.7 load and needs tombstones on delete. Chaining tolerates higher load and simpler deletion. Java upgrades long chains to red-black trees to bound the worst case at O(log n).

cards.prompt: Hash table insert, lookup and delete complexity?
cards.answer: O(1) average, O(n) worst case; O(n) space.
cards.explanation: The worst case needs every key in one bucket — possible with adversarial input, which is why languages randomise string hashing per process (hash-flooding DoS). Ordering is not guaranteed; use a tree map or an insertion-ordered map when it matters.

modules.name: Trees, Heaps & Tries
modules.description: Balanced search trees, priority queues, prefix trees and the structures databases are built on.

cards.prompt: Why does an unbalanced BST matter, and how do balanced trees fix it?
cards.answer: Inserting sorted data into a plain BST produces a linked list — O(n) operations. Self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black) rotate on insert/delete to keep height O(log n).
cards.explanation: AVL is more strictly balanced (faster lookups, more rotations); red-black tolerates more imbalance (faster writes) and is what most standard libraries use for ordered maps. B-trees generalise the idea to high fan-out for disk and page-based storage.

cards.prompt: Why do databases index with B+ trees rather than red-black trees?
cards.answer: Because the cost unit is a disk or page read, not a comparison. A B+ tree node holds hundreds of keys in one page, so tree height is tiny — three or four page reads for millions of rows — and leaves are linked for range scans.
cards.explanation: A red-black tree with a million rows is ~20 levels, meaning up to 20 random reads. A B+ tree with fan-out 500 is 3 levels. Storing all values in the leaves and chaining them also makes `BETWEEN` and `ORDER BY` scans sequential.

resources.title: Use The Index, Luke — Anatomy of an index

cards.prompt: Binary heap: push, pop-min and peek complexity? And building a heap from n items?
cards.answer: Push O(log n), pop O(log n), peek O(1). Heapify from an array is O(n), not O(n log n).

complexity.time: push/pop O(log n), peek O(1), build O(n)

cards.explanation: A binary heap is a complete tree stored in an array: children of i are 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no pointers. The O(n) build works bottom-up — most nodes are near the leaves and sift down only a level or two. It backs Dijkstra, A*, schedulers and top-k.

cards.prompt: You need autocomplete over millions of terms with prefix matching. Which structure, and what is the trade-off?
cards.answer: A trie (prefix tree): lookup and prefix enumeration cost O(k) in the key length, independent of the number of stored keys. The cost is memory — one node per character unless compressed.
cards.explanation: A radix/PATRICIA trie collapses single-child chains and cuts memory dramatically. For static dictionaries, a DAWG or an FST (as used by Lucene) compresses shared suffixes too. A hash map cannot answer prefix queries at all.

cards.answer: List is O(V+E) space and fast to iterate neighbours; matrix is O(V²) space and O(1) edge lookup.

left.title: Adjacency list
points: Right for sparse graphs — most real graphs

right.title: Adjacency matrix
points: Right for dense graphs and small V

cards.explanation: Real-world graphs (social, road, dependency) are sparse: E ≈ cV, so lists win by orders of magnitude. Matrices shine when V is small and bounded, or when you want bitset tricks or Floyd–Warshall.

cards.prompt: What does a disjoint-set (union-find) structure do, and what makes it near-constant time?
cards.answer: It tracks a partition of elements into disjoint sets with `find` (which set?) and `union` (merge two). Path compression plus union by rank/size gives O(α(n)) amortised — inverse Ackermann, effectively constant.
cards.explanation: It powers Kruskal's MST, connected-component labelling, cycle detection in undirected graphs, and incremental connectivity. Path compression flattens the tree during every find, so repeated queries get cheaper as you use it.

cards.prompt: You want to avoid a disk lookup for keys that are definitely absent, using very little memory. What do you use?
cards.answer: A Bloom filter: k hash functions over a bit array. It answers 'definitely not present' or 'possibly present' — false positives are possible, false negatives are not.
cards.explanation: About 10 bits per element gives ~1% false positives. Standard Bloom filters cannot delete (counting variants can) and cannot be resized. LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra and Chrome's safe-browsing all use them to skip expensive lookups.

cards.prompt: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Which two structures do you combine?
cards.answer: A hash map from key to node, plus a doubly linked list ordering nodes by recency. Get moves the node to the head; put evicts the tail when full.
cards.explanation: The hash map gives O(1) lookup, the linked list gives O(1) reordering and eviction — neither can do both alone. This is the canonical 'compose two structures' interview question, and it is exactly how real caches are built.
